theme: Jericho falls; Achan’s sin; Ai taken
readingInstruction: Read Joshua 6:1-8:35. These chapters contain some of the best-known stories in the Old Testament and some of the most uncomfortable. Read slowly through the fall of Jericho, then through Achan’s sin and Israel’s humiliating defeat at Ai, and finally through the renewal of the covenant on Mount Ebal. Ask throughout: what does this show about God’s holiness, and about the seriousness of sin?
settingTheScene: Israel has crossed the Jordan, and the first fortified city stands in the way. Jericho is the gateway to the land. God does not give Joshua a battle plan in the usual sense. He gives him a worship procession. For six days, the army will march around the walls with the ark and seven priests blowing rams’ horns, and on the seventh day they will march seven times and shout. Victory is God’s gift. But right after the high of Jericho comes the low of Ai. A single man’s sin brings defeat on the whole community. These chapters teach that God’s people are called to trust his power and to take his holiness seriously.
observation: The LORD says to Joshua, “See, I have given Jericho into your hand” (6:2). The victory is announced before the battle.
The army marches around the city for six days in silence, and on the seventh day shouts as the walls fall (6:3-20).
Everything in Jericho is placed under the ban (herem) and devoted to the LORD, except Rahab and her family, who are spared (6:17-25).
Achan takes a robe from Shinar, silver, and a bar of gold from the devoted things and hides them in his tent (7:1, 21).
Israel is routed at Ai, and thirty-six men die. Joshua tears his clothes and falls on his face (7:4-6).
The LORD says, “Israel has sinned; they have transgressed my covenant” (7:11). The community is treated as a unit.
Achan is identified by lot, confesses, and is judged along with his family (7:16-26).
After the victory at Ai, Joshua builds an altar on Mount Ebal and reads the blessings and curses of the law to the whole assembly (8:30-35).
interpretation:
The fall of Jericho is a story about who wins battles. No siege equipment, no tactics, no armies are needed. God hands over the city to a people who march, worship, and shout. The point is made so clearly that nobody can miss it: the walls fall by faith. Hebrews 11:30 summarizes it, “By faith the walls of Jericho fell down after they had been encircled for seven days.” The first victory in the land belongs entirely to God. It is also the first fruits of the conquest, and everything in the city is devoted to the LORD.

This is the difficult theme of herem, the ban. Everything in Jericho was to be destroyed. Modern readers rightly feel the weight of this. How can we read it? First, the Bible presents this as a specific, unrepeatable act of divine judgment on a people whose sin had reached its full measure. Genesis 15:16 says that the iniquity of the Amorites was not yet complete in Abraham’s day, which means God waited four hundred years before bringing judgment. Deuteronomy 9:4 says it was “because of the wickedness of these nations” that God drove them out, and warns Israel not to think they are being given the land because of their own righteousness. Second, Jericho is judged and Rahab is saved. The conquest does not teach that Israel is better than its neighbors. It teaches that God is holy, that sin is judged, and that the only safety is to take refuge in him. Third, the command is narrowly bound to the original conquest. The New Testament never uses it as a model for the church. Our weapons are not carnal (2 Corinthians 10:4).

Then chapter 7 shows that this holiness cuts both ways. Achan, an Israelite, takes some of the devoted things. His sin is hidden, but not from God. Israel loses at Ai and thirty-six men die. God’s explanation is frightening: “Israel has sinned.” The community is bound together, and one man’s secret disobedience damages everyone. The text carefully traces Achan’s sin in the verbs of Genesis 3: “I saw… I coveted… I took… I hid” (7:21). He is a second Adam in a garden of promise, and his sin brings death.

Joshua’s response is instructive. He falls on his face, and God tells him to stand up and deal with the sin. Prayer without repentance is not enough. Achan’s judgment is severe, and the valley where it happens is named Achor, meaning “trouble.” But the prophets will later turn the name around. Hosea 2:15 promises that God will make the Valley of Achor “a door of hope.” God’s holiness is not the last word.

The section ends not with a battle but with a covenant renewal. On Mount Ebal and Mount Gerizim, Joshua reads the entire law, blessings and curses, to the people as Moses commanded. The conquest is a covenant event. Israel is not simply taking territory. They are living under the word of the LORD.
connection: The collapse of Jericho is recalled in Hebrews 11:30. Rahab’s rescue ties back to Joshua 2 and forward to Matthew 1:5. The ban’s justification is in Genesis 15:16 and Deuteronomy 9:4-5 and 20:16-18. Achan’s sin echoes Genesis 3:6 and anticipates Ananias and Sapphira in Acts 5. The Valley of Achor reappears in Isaiah 65:10 and Hosea 2:15. The covenant ceremony on Ebal fulfills Deuteronomy 11:29 and 27:1-26.
application:
First, ask what your “walls” might be. Where are you trying to win by effort when God asks you to trust and obey? Take one concrete step of worshipful obedience this week, and leave the outcome with him.

Second, take Achan’s story as a warning about hidden sin. No sin is private. Is there something you are concealing, perhaps a habit, a debt, a relationship, or a resentment? Bring it into the light, first to God, and then to a trusted friend. Concealment is how small sins grow.

Third, remember that Christ is our Joshua. His name is the same in Hebrew. He defeats the powers we cannot overcome, and he is also the one who bore the curse of our sin. Hosea’s “door of hope” is a picture of what he does with our trouble.

Finally, hold both God’s holiness and mercy together. Rahab’s rescue and Achan’s judgment are on the same pages. Both teach us to fear and love him.
prayerPrompts: Ask God to show you any hidden sin and to give you courage to confess it.
Thank him for the victory he gives.
Thank him for turning a valley of trouble into a door of hope.
